1.note: Here, **this word** represents “the message that Yahweh is giving through Amos.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [this message]

Amos is speaking as if the song of mourning that he is singing were a heavy object that he was **lifting up over** the people of Israel. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am singing about you]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **lamentation**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [a mournful song]

Here, **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Israel** means all the people descended from the patriarch Jacob, who was also known as Israel. Alternate translation: [all you Israelites]

2.note: The expression **is forsaken** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Her enemies have left her lying on her land]

Amos is speaking of the nation of Israel being vulnerable as if it were a young **virgin** woman who **has fallen** down and who will never **rise** again. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [The nation of Israel has been defeated; she will never regain her power]

The pronoun **She** refers to the nation of Israel, whom Amos names as **the virgin Israel** later in this verse. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [The nation of Israel has fallen]

Here Amos is speaking of there being no one to help Israel as if it were a woman who had physically “fallen” and no one is **raising her up.** If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly or use a comparable expression. Alternate translation: [there is no one to help her recover]

3.note: Here, **The city** represents “the fighting men who march out from the city.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [A thousand fighting men marching out from a city]
Here, **a thousand** and **a hundred** represent groups of soldiers. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language as modeled in the UST.
See how you translated these same phrases in [5:1](ta:05).

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [to defend the people of Israel]

4.note: Yahweh is speaking as if the people could **Seek** him, as though he were something lost that they could look for and find. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Devote yourselves to me and live]
See how you translated the same phrase “house of Israel” in [5:1](ta:05).

The word translated as **Seek** is an imperative, but it communicates a condition rather than a command. If the imperative does not communicate a condition for your readers, then use a form in your language that communicates a condition. Alternate translation: [If you seek me, then you will live]

5.q: וְ⁠אַֽל־תִּדְרְשׁוּ֙ בֵּֽית־אֵ֔ל וְ⁠הַ⁠גִּלְגָּל֙ לֹ֣א תָבֹ֔אוּ וּ⁠בְאֵ֥ר שֶׁ֖בַע לֹ֣א תַעֲבֹ֑רוּ כִּ֤י הַ⁠גִּלְגָּל֙ גָּלֹ֣ה יִגְלֶ֔ה וּ⁠בֵֽית־אֵ֖ל יִהְיֶ֥ה לְ⁠אָֽוֶן
5.note: Yahweh uses the word **and** here to indicate a contrast between seeking him and seeking the shrines at Bethel, Gilgal, and Beersheba. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [but do not seek Bethel; instead of going to Gilgal or crossing over to Beersheba, remember that Gilgal will surely go into exile, and Bethel will become iniquity.]

Yahweh is speaking of devoting themselves and worshiping at Bethel as if the people could **seek** and find something that had been lost. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and do not devote yourselves to worshiping at Bethel]

Here, **Bethel** represents “the shrine at Bethel where the people worshiped.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the shrine at Bethel]
The words translated as **going into exile, will go into exile** sound like the name of the town, **Gilgal**. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could put this information in a footnote.

Yahweh is repeating forms of the verb **go into exile** in order to intensify his expression of the idea that it conveys. If your language can repeat words for intensification, it would be appropriate to do that here in your translation. If not, your language may have another way of expressing the intensification. Alternate translation: [for Gilgal will certainly go into exile]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **iniquity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and Bethel will become an evil place]

Here, **Bethel** represents “the worship that the people offer at Bethel.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and the worship at Bethel will become iniquity]

6.note: Amos is speaking as if the people could **Seek** Yahweh, as though he were something lost that they could look for and find. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Devote yourselves to Yahweh and live]

Amos is using the word translated as **lest** to introduce an outcome that he does not want to happen. Because of this, he first gives the people of Israel an instruction to follow so that this will not happen. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that avoiding this outcome is the purpose of the instruction. Alternate translation: [otherwise, he will break out]

The point of this comparison is that just as **fire** spreads swiftly and destroys everything in its path, so Yahweh’s judgment will come swiftly and destroy the descendants of Joseph. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [lest he break out against the house of Joseph like a fire that spreads swiftly and destroys everything in its path]

Here the term **house** means all the people descended from a particular person. It envisions them as if they were one household living together. So **the house of Joseph** means all the people descended from the patriarch Joseph. By this time, those descendants had become the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh. Alternate translation: [among the descendants of Joseph] or [among the people of the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh]

is speaking as if Yahweh’s judgment against them were a **fire** that **consumes** them. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and his judgment will destroy Bethel, and no one will be able to stop it]
The pronoun **it** refers to the **fire** that Yahweh will send. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the fire consumes]

7.note: Amos is speaking to those who have distorted justice as if **justice** were something that they could change into **wormwood**, a poisonous plant with a very bitter taste. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [those who have distorted justice for people]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the ones turning what is just into something bitter]

Amos is speaking of rejecting righteousness as if **righteousness** were an object that these people could **cast** down **to the ground** and leave there. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they completely reject righteousness]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and they cast what is right to the ground]

8.q: עֹשֵׂ֨ה כִימָ֜ה וּ⁠כְסִ֗יל וְ⁠הֹפֵ֤ךְ לַ⁠בֹּ֨קֶר֙ צַלְמָ֔וֶת וְ⁠י֖וֹם לַ֣יְלָה הֶחְשִׁ֑יךְ הַ⁠קּוֹרֵ֣א לְ⁠מֵֽי־הַ⁠יָּ֗ם וַֽ⁠יִּשְׁפְּכֵ֛⁠ם עַל־פְּנֵ֥י הָ⁠אָ֖רֶץ יְהוָ֥ה שְׁמֽ⁠וֹ
8.note: Amos describes Yahweh as the one with power over all he created by a series of phrases and only names him at the end of the verse. If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about who Yahweh is before the information about what he does. Alternate translation: [Yahweh is the maker of the Pleiades and Orion, turning deep darkness into morning; he darkens day into night; calling for the waters of the sea, he pours them out on the face of the earth.]

The terms **Pleiades** and **Orion** are the names of groups of stars in the night sky. If your readers would not be familiar with what these are, you could use the names of star groups that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the groups of stars in the sky]

8.q: וְ⁠הֹפֵ֤ךְ לַ⁠בֹּ֨קֶר֙ צַלְמָ֔וֶת וְ⁠י֖וֹם לַ֣יְלָה הֶחְשִׁ֑יךְ
8.note: Amos is referring to all of time by naming the two major components, **morning** and **night**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [governing the passing of all time, from morning until night]

Amos is using **the face of the earth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “the surface of the earth.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [everywhere on the earth]
Amos is using the term **name** to represent who the Yahweh is or to refer to the Yahweh’s reputation. Alternate translation: [This is Yahweh himself]

9.note: Amos is speaking destroying the strong as if **destruction** were lightning that Yahweh could make **flash** suddenly against strong people. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the one bringing sudden ruin upon the strong]

9.q: הַ⁠מַּבְלִ֥יג שֹׁ֖ד עַל־עָ֑ז וְ⁠שֹׁ֖ד עַל & יָבֽוֹא
9.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **destruction**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the one suddenly destroying the strong, and he destroys]

Amos is using the adjective **strong** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [against those who are strong]

10.note: The pronoun **They** refers to the strong referred to in the previous verse, or those who are influential people of Israel whom Amos is condemning. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Those of you who are strong hate the reprover in the gate]

Here, **the gate** represents “the place where the leaders of a city decided legal cases.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the reprover at the place of judgment]

11.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **trampling**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [because you trample on the poor]

The implication is that these are **vineyards** that are pleasant and desirable. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [delightful vineyards]

Amos is speaking those who are mistreating poor people as if these people were **trampling on the poor** beneath their feet. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [you are mistreating the poor]

Amos is using the adjective **poor** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are poor]

12.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **transgressions** and **sins**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [that you have done many bad things and that you have sinned greatly]

The terms **transgressions** and **sins** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [your sins are very many and very great]

Yahweh is using the adjective **righteous** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [righteous people]

Yahweh is speaking of those who deny justice to poor people as if they physically **turn aside the needy** so that they cannot reach the **gate**, the place where legal cases are decided. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they deny justice to the needy]

Amos is using the adjective **needy** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [needy people]

Here, **the gate** represents “the place where the leaders of a city decided legal cases.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [at the place where legal cases are decided]

13.note: Amos is using the adjective **prudent** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [those who are wise]

The word translated as **will be still** could mean: (1) “will be quiet.” That is, prudent people will avoid criticizing people who do evil because doing so would be futile. Alternate translation: [will be silent] or (2) “will cease.” This would mean that prudent people will cease, that is, that there will be no more prudent people. Alternate translation: [will cease] or [will not be found]

14.note: Amos is speaking of trying to do something good or evil as if **good** and **evil** were objects someone would actually go search for or **seek**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Try to do what is good, and not what is evil]

The word translated as **thus** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [as a result,]

Amos is using this possessive form to mean the God who commands the armies of heaven. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [God who commands the armies of heaven]

15.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and judge fairly in the gate]

Here, **the gate** represents “the place where the leaders of a city decided legal cases.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and establish justice in the place where the city leaders judge legal cases]

This part of the verse introduces the possible consequence of fulfilling the condition proposed in the previous part. Use a natural form in your language for introducing the possible consequence of fulfilling this condition. Alternate translation: [if you do all those things, then perhaps, Yahweh]
See how you translated this same phrase, “God of Armies,” in 5:14.

Amos is presenting a possible situation, that Yahweh **will be gracious** to the survivors of the northern kingdom if the people hate evil, love good, and establish justice. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [if you do these things, then perhaps Yahweh, God of Armies, may be gracious]

Amos is using the possessive form to describe a **remnant** that is made up of the remaining descendants of **Joseph**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to those who survive among the descendants of Joseph]

16.note: See how you translated this same phrase, “God of Armies,” in 5:14.

Yahweh is describing people using a word, **Alas**, that expresses a strong feeling of dismay and distress. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [Oh no! Oh no!] or [What a disaster!]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context of the previous phrase if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and they will call those knowing a lament to wailing]

17.note: Yahweh assumes that readers would understand that the words **pass through** meant that he would be coming among them to punish them. You could say that explicitly if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [I will come among you and punish you]

Amos is using the phrase **says Yahweh** to indicate that what has been said is a direct quotation from Yahweh and comes with Yahweh’s authority. In your translation, use a natural way of indicating direct quotations in your language.

18.note: Amos is using a phrase, **Woe to**, that expresses a strong feeling of grief and warning about coming disaster. There may be an equivalent word or phrase in your language that you can use in your translation to convey this feeling. Alternate translation: [How dreadful it will be for those desiring]

Amos knows that his readers thought of **the day of Yahweh** as a time when Yahweh will come to bring justice but they thought it was to judge their enemies, not themselves. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the time when Yahweh will come to bring justice]

Amos is using the question form to rebuke his hearers for wanting **the day of Yahweh** to come. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The day of Yahweh will bring you no benefit!]

Amos is speaking as if disaster were **darkness** and deliverance were **light**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [It is a day of disaster and not of deliverance]
The pronoun **It** refers to **the day of Yahweh**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [That day is darkness and not light]

19.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **a man** who escapes one deadly danger runs straight into another, so the people of Israel will find no escape when Yahweh judges them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [You will be as unable to escape as a man who flees from the face of the lion]
Here, **the face** represents “the presence.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [from the presence of the lion]
The pronoun **him** refers to the man who is fleeing from the lion. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the bear meets that man]

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [or as when a man goes into the house]

The implication is that the man goes **into the house** in order to be safe, but that even there he meets deadly danger. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [rests his hand on the wall, thinking he is now safe, and the snake bites him]

20.q: הֲ⁠לֹא־חֹ֛שֶׁךְ י֥וֹם יְהוָ֖ה וְ⁠לֹא־א֑וֹר וְ⁠אָפֵ֖ל וְ⁠לֹא־נֹ֥גַֽהּ לֽ⁠וֹ
20.note: Amos is using the question form to emphasize that **the day of Yahweh** will certainly bring disaster and nothing good. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [The day of Yahweh is darkness, and not light, and gloom, with no brightness in it!]
See how you translated the similar expression in 5:18.

Amos is speaking as if disaster were **darkness** and **gloom** and as if deliverance were **light** and **brightness**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [disaster, and not deliverance? Even sorrow, with no relief]

Amos is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [Is the day of Yahweh not even gloom, with no brightness in it]

21.note: This is the beginning of what Yahweh said. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could mark that this is a direct quote of Yahweh as in the UST.

The terms **hate** and **reject** mean similar things. Yahweh is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [I reject with utter hatred]

Here, Yahweh uses **smell** to represent his accepting the pleasing aroma of the smoke that ascended from the burnt sacrifices. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [and I will take no pleasure in the sacrifices you offer at your assemblies]

22.note: Yahweh is presenting a possible situation, that the people might **offer up** to him **burnt offerings** and grain offerings. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. Alternate translation: [For suppose you offer up to me burnt offerings]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **peace offering** that is made from **your fattened animals**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and the peace offering that you make from your fattened animals]

Here, **look at** represents regarding something with favor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will not regard with favor]

Yahweh is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [I will not look at your peace offerings]

23.note: Here, **your songs and the music of your harps** represent “the worship that you offer to me.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the noise of the worship you offer me]

Here, **hear** represents “accept” or “pay attention to.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [I will not accept as worship]

24.note: The point of this comparison is that just as **waters** flow abundantly and spread everywhere, so **justice** should be abundant and spread everywhere among the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [But let justice spread everywhere like waters]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **justice**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [people treating each other justly]

The point of this comparison is that just as **an ever-flowing stream** never stops, so **righteousness** should be constantly among the people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and righteousness flowing constantly like a stream that never stops]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **righteousness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and doing what is right]

25.q: הַ⁠זְּבָחִ֨ים וּ⁠מִנְחָ֜ה הִֽגַּשְׁתֶּם־לִ֧⁠י בַ⁠מִּדְבָּ֛ר אַרְבָּעִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה
25.note: Yahweh is using the question form to challenge the assumption of the people that sacrifices are all that he requires of them when actually, what he wants is their love and obedience. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [You did not bring near to me sacrifices and grain offerings in the wilderness forty years, house of Israel.]

The pronoun **you** refers to the ancestors of the Israelites being addressed who lived during the years **in the wilderness**. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [Did your ancestors bring near to me]
See how you translated the similar expression in [5:1](ta:05).

26.q: אֵ֚ת סִכּ֣וּת מַלְכְּ⁠כֶ֔ם וְ⁠אֵ֖ת כִּיּ֣וּן צַלְמֵי⁠כֶ֑ם כּוֹכַב֙ אֱלֹ֣הֵי⁠כֶ֔ם
26.note: **Sikkuth** and **Kiyyun** are the names of gods that the people of other nations worshiped that the Israelites also worshiped. If your readers would not be familiar with what these are, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the statue of the god you called your king, and the image of another star-god you worshiped]

The pronoun **which** refers to the images of the gods that the people carried. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [which images of your gods you made for yourselves]

By **the star of your gods**, Yahweh is further clarifying that **Kiyyun** is the false god that they worshiped that is represented by a star. You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [the god that you worship that is represented by a star]

27.note: The word translated as **So** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a result of what came before. Alternate translation: [Because you did those things, I will exile you]

Yahweh assumes that readers would have known that **farther than Damascus** represented all the lands far to the north and east, where Assyria rules. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [to the distant lands ruled by Assyria]
See how you translated this same phrase, “Yahweh, God of Armies is his name” in 4:13. Alternate translation: [Yahweh, who is God of Armies]
